result.summary: Pausanias traces how Lysimachus held Thrace and won Macedonia after wars with Demetrius and Pyrrhus. He then tells how his marriage to Arsinoe led to the death of his son Agathocles, the defection of his supporters, and his own defeat and death against Seleucus.

scenes.title: Lysimachus's wars for Macedonia
scenes.summary: Lysimachus fights Demetrius, keeps Thrace with Pyrrhus's help, and later drives Pyrrhus out of Macedonia after Demetrius falls to Seleucus.
scenes.stakes: Lysimachus risks losing Thrace and his place among the successors to rival kings.

scenes.title: Arsinoe plots against Agathocles
scenes.summary: Lysimachus marries Arsinoe, who plots the death of his son Agathocles. Lysandra flees with her children and kin.
scenes.stakes: Agathocles faces death, and Lysimachus loses his friends and his family's loyalty.

scenes.title: Fall and burial of Lysimachus
scenes.summary: The exiles urge Seleucus to war and Philetærus gives him Pergamum and money. Lysimachus is beaten and killed, and his son Alexander buries him in the Chersonese.
scenes.stakes: Lysimachus stands to lose his kingdom and his life in battle with Seleucus.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' moral framing of the story: love brings many misfortunes to men.

analysis.text: The passage shows how ambition and family passion destroyed a successful ruler, with love and jealousy driving the fall of Lysimachus.
It records the power struggles among Alexander the Great's successors in the early third century BC.

fun_facts.text: Philetærus' takeover of Pergamum began the Attalid dynasty, which later ruled a major Hellenistic kingdom.

language_notes.text: "Grasping something" means being greedy for more territory; Demetrius's acquisitiveness is called a family trait, inherited from Antigonus.
"Within an ace of" is an idiom meaning very nearly; Lysimachus almost lost Thrace entirely.
The sentence is confusing: Lysandra first flees to Seleucus, then the exiles are said to take refuge with Ptolemy, her kin, so the narrative is compressed.
Pergamum, a fortress city near the river Caicus, was where Lysimachus kept his treasure; Philetærus later founded the Pergamene dynasty there.
The Chersonese is the Thracian peninsula (Gallipoli) along the Hellespont; Cardia was a city at its neck.

context_notes.text: Lysimachus was one of Alexander the Great's generals who became king of Thrace after Alexander's death; the Successors fought constantly over Macedonia.
Seleucus, another of Alexander's generals, ruled much of Asia. Demetrius ended as his captive after failing in Asia.
Arsinoe was a daughter of Ptolemy I of Egypt; her marriage to the aged Lysimachus set up the dynastic rivalry that follows.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias interrupts the political narrative with a moralizing generalization, introducing the domestic tragedy as a lesson about love.
Lysimachus learns the truth only when it is too late and he is friendless, a bitter reversal for a victorious king.
The brief, summarizing final line closes the king's story with a flat note of fate, in the manner of a tragic conclusion.
